title: Food ordering (Swiggy-like)
scopeHtml: Scope: cart, order state machine, observer notifications, driver assignment, CAS on status.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design the order flow of a Swiggy-like app: browse a restaurant menu, fill a cart, place an order, track its status, and assign a delivery partner.

Clarify:

  • Functional: menu, cart (one restaurant at a time), place order, status changes, driver assignment, notifications.
  • Rules: an order moves through fixed states; you cannot cancel after pickup.
  • Out of scope: live map, payments, ratings, search ranking.
  • Scale talk: Swiggy handles on the order of millions of orders a day, with a dinner peak of a few thousand orders per second city-wide; per-order logic is still tiny.

Worked example. 2 Biryani at 250 plus 1 Raita at 40 gives 540. A dinner peak of 3,000 orders per second spread over 10,000 restaurants is under 1 order per second per restaurant: no hot spot at that level.

Industry examples. Swiggy and Zomato model orders as a state machine and push each transition as an event to Kafka, which drives push notifications, restaurant tablets and the delivery app. DoorDash has published on its dispatch (assignment) system as an optimisation problem, not a simple nearest-driver rule.

Everyday analogy. A parcel tracking page: each stage is a fixed step and you cannot jump from "packed" to "delivered".

Common interview traps.

  • Letting status be a free string that any code can overwrite.
  • Mixing carts from two restaurants.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Restaurant with a Menu of MenuItem (id, name, price).
  • Cart: lines of item and quantity, total.
  • Order: id, amount, status, driver, listeners.
  • OrderStatus: PLACED, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED, CANCELLED.
  • DriverAssignment strategy and FoodService that coordinates.

Decision gravity. Cart total is computed at order time and frozen into Order.amount; later menu price changes must not alter old orders. Reversible: no once you have real orders, so snapshot prices from day one.

Everyday analogy. A receipt: prices are printed when you pay, not recalculated tomorrow.

Common interview traps.

  • Referencing live menu prices from old orders.
  • Using double for price.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
Restaurant 1---* MenuItem
Cart ---------> Restaurant
Cart 1---* (MenuItem, qty)

FoodService ---creates---> Order
FoodService ---uses-----> <<DriverAssignment>>  <|-- FirstFree, Nearest
Order --has--> OrderStatus
Order 1---* <<OrderListener>>   (push, SMS, restaurant tablet)

Order.moveTo(next): checks NEXT[status] contains next, then notifies listeners

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing listeners as part of Order's logic instead of an interface.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• State machine (enum plus allowed-transitions map): one place decides legality. Alternative: the full State pattern with a class per state, worth it only when each state has very different behaviour. Reversible: yes.
  • Observer (OrderListener): customer push, restaurant screen and analytics all react to a status change without Order knowing them. At scale this becomes a Kafka topic.
  • Strategy for driver assignment: first-free today, nearest or batching tomorrow.
  • Not used: Singleton for FoodService; pass it in instead so tests can create their own.

Worked example. ACCEPTED to CANCELLED allowed; PICKED_UP to CANCELLED rejected with IllegalStateException. A refund policy hangs off the second rule.

Industry examples. Stripe's PaymentIntent and Uber trip states are the same idea: explicit states with a table of legal moves.

Everyday analogy. A traffic light: green cannot jump to red without going through amber.

Common interview traps.

  • Switch statements on status scattered across the codebase.
  • Calling listeners inside a lock (a slow listener blocks everyone).

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
import java.util.*;

enum OrderStatus { PLACED, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED, CANCELLED }

record MenuItem(String id, String name, long price) {}

class Restaurant {
    final String name; final Map<String, MenuItem> menu = new HashMap<>();
    Restaurant(String n) { name = n; }
    Restaurant add(MenuItem m) { menu.put(m.id(), m); return this; }
}

class Cart {
    final Restaurant restaurant; final Map<MenuItem, Integer> lines = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    Cart(Restaurant r) { restaurant = r; }
    void add(String itemId, int qty) {
        MenuItem m = restaurant.menu.get(itemId);
        if (m == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not on menu");
        lines.merge(m, qty, Integer::sum);
    }
    long total() { long t = 0; for (var e : lines.entrySet()) t += e.getKey().price() * e.getValue(); return t; }
}

interface OrderListener { void onStatus(Order o, OrderStatus s); }

class Order {
    private static final Map<OrderStatus, Set<OrderStatus>> NEXT = Map.of(
        OrderStatus.PLACED, Set.of(OrderStatus.ACCEPTED, OrderStatus.CANCELLED),
        OrderStatus.ACCEPTED, Set.of(OrderStatus.PREPARING, OrderStatus.CANCELLED),
        OrderStatus.PREPARING, Set.of(OrderStatus.PICKED_UP),
        OrderStatus.PICKED_UP, Set.of(OrderStatus.DELIVERED),
        OrderStatus.DELIVERED, Set.of(), OrderStatus.CANCELLED, Set.of());
    final String id; final long amount; String driver;
    private OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.PLACED;
    private final List<OrderListener> listeners = new ArrayList<>();
    Order(String id, long amount) { this.id = id; this.amount = amount; }
    void subscribe(OrderListener l) { listeners.add(l); }
    OrderStatus status() { return status; }
    void moveTo(OrderStatus s) {
        if (!NEXT.get(status).contains(s)) throw new IllegalStateException(status + " -> " + s);
        status = s;
        for (OrderListener l : listeners) l.onStatus(this, s);
    }
}

interface DriverAssignment { String pick(List<String> freeDrivers); }
class FirstFree implements DriverAssignment {
    public String pick(List<String> d) { return d.isEmpty() ? null : d.get(0); }
}

class FoodService {
    private final List<String> freeDrivers = new ArrayList<>(List.of("D1", "D2"));
    private final DriverAssignment assign;
    private int seq = 0;
    FoodService(DriverAssignment a) { assign = a; }
    Order place(Cart c) {
        if (c.lines.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("empty cart");
        return new Order("O" + (++seq), c.total());
    }
    void dispatch(Order o) {
        String d = assign.pick(freeDrivers);
        if (d == null) throw new IllegalStateException("no driver");
        freeDrivers.remove(d); o.driver = d;
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Restaurant r = new Restaurant("Biryani House")
            .add(new MenuItem("b1", "Biryani", 250)).add(new MenuItem("r1", "Raita", 40));
        Cart c = new Cart(r); c.add("b1", 2); c.add("r1", 1);
        FoodService svc = new FoodService(new FirstFree());
        Order o = svc.place(c);
        o.subscribe((ord, s) -> System.out.println(ord.id + " is " + s));
        System.out.println("total " + o.amount);
        o.moveTo(OrderStatus.ACCEPTED); o.moveTo(OrderStatus.PREPARING);
        svc.dispatch(o); o.moveTo(OrderStatus.PICKED_UP); o.moveTo(OrderStatus.DELIVERED);
        try { o.moveTo(OrderStatus.CANCELLED); throw new AssertionError(); }
        catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("illegal: " + e.getMessage()); }
    }
}

Kotlin core:

enum class Status { PLACED, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED, CANCELLED }

private val next = mapOf(
    Status.PLACED to setOf(Status.ACCEPTED, Status.CANCELLED),
    Status.ACCEPTED to setOf(Status.PREPARING, Status.CANCELLED),
    Status.PREPARING to setOf(Status.PICKED_UP),
    Status.PICKED_UP to setOf(Status.DELIVERED),
    Status.DELIVERED to emptySet(), Status.CANCELLED to emptySet())

class Order(val id: String, val amount: Long) {
    var status = Status.PLACED; private set
    private val listeners = mutableListOf<(Order, Status) -> Unit>()
    fun subscribe(l: (Order, Status) -> Unit) { listeners += l }
    fun moveTo(s: Status) {
        check(s in next.getValue(status)) { "$status -> $s" }
        status = s
        listeners.forEach { it(this, s) }
    }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to validate that the item belongs to this restaurant.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac -d out Main.java
java -cp out Main
total 540
O1 is ACCEPTED
O1 is PREPARING
O1 is PICKED_UP
O1 is DELIVERED
illegal: DELIVERED -> CANCELLED

Test: illegal jumps, empty cart, unknown item, no driver free, price frozen after menu change.

Common interview traps.

  • Not testing the illegal transitions, which are the whole point.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Races to name:

  1. Restaurant clicks Accept while customer clicks Cancel: both read PLACED, both write. One wins silently.
  2. Two orders grab the same last free driver.
  3. Listeners run on the caller thread.

Thread-safe version. Make moveTo atomic with a compare-and-set on the status, and the driver pool a concurrent queue.

class Order {
    private final AtomicReference<OrderStatus> status = new AtomicReference<>(OrderStatus.PLACED);
    private final List<OrderListener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    boolean moveTo(OrderStatus next) {
        while (true) {
            OrderStatus cur = status.get();
            if (!NEXT.get(cur).contains(next)) throw new IllegalStateException(cur + " -> " + next);
            if (status.compareAndSet(cur, next)) {          // loser of a race retries and then sees the new state
                for (OrderListener l : listeners) l.onStatus(this, next);
                return true;
            }
        }
    }
}

class FoodService {
    private final ConcurrentLinkedQueue<String> freeDrivers = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
    void dispatch(Order o) {
        String d = freeDrivers.poll();                      // atomic: no two orders get the same driver
        if (d == null) throw new IllegalStateException("no driver");
        o.driver = d;
    }
}

In the Accept vs Cancel race, whoever CASes first wins; the other retries, finds PREPARING or CANCELLED, and gets an exception the API turns into HTTP 409.

Production note (gravity). Across servers use the database: UPDATE orders SET status='ACCEPTED' WHERE id=? AND status='PLACED', check affected rows is 1. That is a compare-and-set in SQL and the standard answer. Dispatch listeners asynchronously (queue) so a slow SMS gateway cannot block a state change.

Common interview traps.

  • Using synchronized on a method and then calling listeners inside it.
  • Believing in-JVM CAS protects against two app servers.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Nearest driver: new DriverAssignment using distance; later batching two orders per driver.
  • Scheduled orders and surge pricing: more Strategies.
  • Restaurant timeout: auto-cancel if not accepted in 3 minutes (needs a scheduler, see P19).
  • Coupons and taxes on the cart: Decorator or a list of PriceRules.
  • Partial refunds and substitutions.

Common interview traps.

  • Solving timeouts with Thread.sleep per order.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Order status is a state machine with an explicit transition table.
  • Observer fan-out for notifications; Strategy for driver assignment.
  • Snapshot prices in the order; money as long.
  • Concurrency: CAS on status (or conditional SQL UPDATE), atomic driver pool.
  • Notify listeners outside locks and asynchronously.

questions.promptHtml: Why model order status as a state machine with a transition table instead of a free string or enum that any code can set?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you protect invariants in one place and know how real order flows (Swiggy, Uber, Stripe) behave.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An order has fixed legal moves: PLACED to ACCEPTED or CANCELLED, ACCEPTED to PREPARING or CANCELLED, PREPARING to PICKED_UP, PICKED_UP to DELIVERED. I keep a map of allowed next states and a single moveTo(next) method that checks the map and then notifies listeners. That way illegal jumps (DELIVERED to CANCELLED, PREPARING to DELIVERED) are impossible, and one place decides legality instead of switch statements scattered everywhere.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Enum plus a Map<Status, Set<Status>> is enough; the full State pattern (class per state) is worth it only if each state has very different behaviour.
  • The transition table is also the documentation: cancellation after pickup is simply absent.
  • Exceptions on illegal moves become HTTP 409 at the API.
PLACED -> ACCEPTED -> PREPARING -> PICKED_UP -> DELIVERED
   \          \
    -> CANCELLED <-   (no cancel after PREPARING)

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void moveTo(OrderStatus s) {
    if (!NEXT.get(status).contains(s)) throw new IllegalStateException(status + " -> " + s);
    status = s;
    for (OrderListener l : listeners) l.onStatus(this, s);
}
fun moveTo(s: Status) {
    check(s in next.getValue(status)) { "$status -> $s" }
    status = s
    listeners.forEach { it(this, s) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Status as a public mutable field or a free string.
  • switch on status duplicated in many classes.
  • No tests for illegal transitions, which are the point.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When would you use the State pattern? -> When each state has substantially different behaviour and data.
  2. What does cancellation after PREPARING mean? -> Business rule: a partial refund or a restaurant-confirmed cancel; model as a new transition or a separate flow.
  3. How do you test it? -> A table test of all pairs: legal ones pass, illegal ones throw.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use an enum for status". Senior: a transition table enforced in one method, atomic moves under concurrency, events emitted on each move.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team let services write status strings directly; an order was marked DELIVERED then PREPARING by two racing consumers and the customer was charged twice.

questions.contextHtml:
A cart from "Biryani House" can include an item from another restaurant, and the support team sees duplicate push notifications. Code under review:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Cart {
    final Map<String, Integer> lines = new HashMap<>();      // itemId -> qty
    void add(String itemId, int qty) { lines.merge(itemId, qty, Integer::sum); }
    double total() { double t = 0; for (var e : lines.entrySet()) t += PRICES.get(e.getKey()) * e.getValue(); return t; }
}
class Order {
    String status = "PLACED";
    final List<OrderListener> listeners = new ArrayList<>();
    void setStatus(String s) {
        status = s;
        for (OrderListener l : listeners) l.onStatus(this, s);
    }
}
class Cart {
    val lines = HashMap<String, Int>()
    fun add(itemId: String, qty: Int) { lines.merge(itemId, qty, Int::plus) }
    fun total(): Double = lines.entries.sumOf { PRICES.getValue(it.key) * it.value }
}
class Order {
    var status = "PLACED"
    val listeners = mutableListOf<OrderListener>()
    fun setStatus(s: String) { status = s; listeners.forEach { it.onStatus(this, s) } }
}
questions.promptHtml: List all defects and say how to fix each.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices only the double. Does not connect the status setter to duplicate notifications.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: One restaurant per cart? Do prices change? Can setStatus be called by multiple services?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I would block the review as correctness bugs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The cart does not know its restaurant, so items from another restaurant can be added. (b) double for money. (c) Total is computed with live prices; no snapshot when the order is placed. (d) setStatus accepts any string and any move, so repeated or illegal updates notify listeners repeatedly (duplicate pushes); setStatus("PLACED") twice sends twice. (e) ArrayList of listeners and listeners called in the caller's thread.
  4. How I'd verify: Tests: add item from the wrong menu throws; setting the same status twice does not double-notify; totals equal exact paise.
  5. Root cause: No invariants at the boundaries.
  6. Fix: Cart(Restaurant r) validating each item against r.menu; total as long price x qty; Order.moveTo(next) with a transition table that throws on illegal or repeated moves; notify only after a successful move.
  7. Prevention: Table-driven transition tests; ban String statuses by review rule; contract: services call moveTo, never set fields.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not silently ignore repeats as a fix for duplicates: reject or treat as idempotent no-op explicitly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same item, price differs between menu versions? -> Snapshot price into the order lines at placement.
  • Listener throws? -> Catch and log per listener so one failure does not block others.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident where a retry loop re-set the same status and customers got six push notifications for one order.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixes double only.
  • Hire: cart restaurant validation, transition table, long money.
  • Strong hire: idempotency of repeats, snapshot prices, listener failure isolation.

questions.contextHtml: At 20:15 a customer taps Cancel on order O-9912 at the same moment the restaurant taps Accept. Logs show: 20:15:03.120 O-9912 PLACED -> ACCEPTED (restaurant) and 20:15:03.121 O-9912 PLACED -> CANCELLED (customer). The final status is CANCELLED, but the restaurant is cooking and the driver was dispatched. The moveTo implementation validates against the current status and then assigns it, without any lock.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the race and give a fix that works on one JVM, then on several app servers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Makes the method synchronized and claims it works across servers, or calls listeners inside the lock.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: One app server or many? What should win: accept or cancel? What does the loser see (HTTP 409)? Is a refund involved?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For this order, contact the restaurant and either honour the cancellation (refund) or reverse; for the system, serialize status changes per order.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Check-then-act without atomicity: both calls read PLACED, both pass validation, last write wins silently. (b) Listeners ran before the status write settled. (c) Clock skew in log timestamps: red herring.
  4. How I'd verify: Two-thread test hammering moveTo(ACCEPTED) and moveTo(CANCELLED) on a fresh order, asserting exactly one wins and the loser gets an exception.
  5. Root cause: Non-atomic read-validate-write on status.
  6. Fix (single JVM): AtomicReference<OrderStatus> with a compare-and-set loop:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
boolean moveTo(OrderStatus next) {
    while (true) {
        OrderStatus cur = status.get();
        if (!NEXT.get(cur).contains(next)) throw new IllegalStateException(cur + " -> " + next);
        if (status.compareAndSet(cur, next)) {
            for (OrderListener l : listeners) l.onStatus(this, next);
            return true;
        }
    }
}
fun moveTo(next: Status): Boolean {
    while (true) {
        val cur = status.get()
        check(next in transitions.getValue(cur)) { "$cur -> $next" }
        if (status.compareAndSet(cur, next)) { listeners.forEach { it(this, next) }; return true }
    }
}

The loser retries, sees ACCEPTED, and ACCEPTED to CANCELLED is legal but PREPARING to CANCELLED is not: it gets a clean exception that the API maps to HTTP 409. Across servers: UPDATE orders SET status='ACCEPTED' WHERE id=? AND status='PLACED', then check rows affected equals 1; the DB is the arbiter. 7. Prevention: Concurrency test; log the transition with actor and previous state; metric on 409 rate. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not call listeners inside a lock (a slow SMS gateway would block status changes), and I would not believe in-JVM CAS protects across servers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cancel after accept should be allowed with a fee? -> Another transition rule; the CAS still guards it.
  • Retry storm on conflicts? -> Bounded retries; the loop above terminates because states are monotonic.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where a status race produced orders that were both "cancelled" and "delivered", requiring manual refund review.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: plain synchronized with listeners inside.
  • Hire: CAS or conditional SQL update, 409 on loser.
  • Strong hire: multi-server reasoning, listener isolation, monotonic-state termination, audit log.

questions.contextHtml: Support gets tickets: "I paid 540 but my order page now shows 640" and finance finds revenue reports changing after the restaurant edited its menu. The order stores only restaurantId, a list of (itemId, qty) and computes total() by reading the current menu price. 2.4 million orders per day; about 5% of restaurants edit prices daily.
questions.promptHtml: Why is this happening, how do you fix it, and what about old data?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds a cache to hold old prices or tells support to explain it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we have price history? Who reads order totals (UI, payments, reports)? Are taxes and discounts also derived?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the bleeding: from now on write unitPrice and amount into the order at placement; for old orders, backfill from price history if available.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The order references live menu prices (root cause). (b) Float rounding in totals: a distraction. (c) Cache staleness: no, since the data really changed.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare order.amount_at_payment with recomputed total for sampled orders; check which orders differ.
  5. Root cause: Derived data presented as historical fact.
  6. Fix: The order line stores itemName, unitPrice (paise as long) and qty, plus amount. Totals never read the menu again. Backfill: join with menu change log by timestamp; where unknown, use the payment record amount as the source of truth.
  7. Prevention: A test: place order, edit menu price, re-read order: amount unchanged; schema review rule that order and payment tables never join to mutable catalogue prices.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Duplicating names and prices uses more storage (about 100 bytes per line; at 2.4M orders x 3 lines = 720 MB/day to verify against your schema), which is fine; I would not rebuild totals from the live menu or keep versions of the whole menu forever for this.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Restaurant changes price between cart and payment? -> Lock the cart price at checkout and show a confirmation if the price changed.
  • Taxes change? -> Snapshot tax rate in the order as well.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where a monthly report was re-run after a menu update and finance spent two days reconciling revenue that had silently changed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cache or manual explanations.
  • Hire: snapshot in order lines, backfill plan.
  • Strong hire: payment record as truth, cart-to-checkout price change UX, storage math, tests and schema rule.

questions.contextHtml: Operations wants driver assignment to use distance (nearest free driver within 3 km), later to batch two orders per driver. Currently DriverAssignment.pick(List<String> freeDrivers) returns the first free driver. The product also wants a fallback: if nobody is within 3 km, widen to 5 km and retry after 30 seconds.
questions.promptHtml: What changes in the design, and what interface do you define?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Rewrites FoodService.dispatch with distance maths inline, making batching another rewrite.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where do driver locations come from (a location service)? How fresh? Can a driver have more than one active order? What is the objective (shortest pickup, fairness, delivery time)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; keep FirstFree as the fallback implementation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The seam is already Strategy. The current interface lacks the data to decide: it needs the order and the driver candidates with locations.
  4. How I'd verify: Unit tests with fixed coordinates: nearest chosen; none within radius returns empty; ties broken by id.
  5. Root cause / design: Change the interface to Optional<Driver> pick(Order o, List<Driver> candidates); Driver(id, lat, lon). Implementations: FirstFree, Nearest(radiusKm), later BatchingAssignment. FoodService only calls the strategy and handles "none".
  6. Fix (code):

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface DriverAssignment { Optional<Driver> pick(Order o, List<Driver> free); }

class Nearest implements DriverAssignment {
    private final double radiusKm; Nearest(double r) { radiusKm = r; }
    public Optional<Driver> pick(Order o, List<Driver> free) {
        return free.stream().filter(d -> Geo.km(d, o.restaurant()) <= radiusKm)
                   .min(Comparator.comparingDouble(d -> Geo.km(d, o.restaurant())));
    }
}
fun interface DriverAssignment { fun pick(o: Order, free: List<Driver>): Driver? }

class Nearest(private val radiusKm: Double) : DriverAssignment {
    override fun pick(o: Order, free: List<Driver>) =
        free.filter { Geo.km(it, o.restaurant) <= radiusKm }.minByOrNull { Geo.km(it, o.restaurant) }
}
  1. Prevention: Test with edge distances (exactly 3 km); log assignment decisions for offline evaluation.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Nearest-driver is a greedy heuristic; real dispatch systems treat assignment as an optimisation over many orders and drivers (DoorDash has published on this), so keep the interface free to evolve. I would not tie assignment to a Thread.sleep retry: schedule a retry task (see timeout scheduling).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two orders choose the same nearest driver simultaneously? -> The claim must be atomic (poll from a concurrent pool or conditional update on driver state).
  • Batching? -> The strategy receives open orders too: input is a set of orders and candidates.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where the first nearest-driver rollout starved far-away orders because the strategy always picked the closest driver and never widened.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: inline distance in the service.
  • Hire: richer Strategy interface and new implementations, no FoodService change.
  • Strong hire: atomic claim, retry widening, heuristic vs optimisation awareness, test edges.

questions.subtopic: Observer inside vs outside the lock
questions.promptHtml: Why should OrderListener callbacks not run inside a lock, and what do you do at Swiggy scale?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests the Observer pattern's operational consequences: slow subscribers, ordering and failure isolation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Listeners (push, SMS, restaurant tablet, analytics) are unknown code. If I call them inside a synchronized method or while holding a lock, one slow SMS gateway blocks every status change for that lock. So I change the state first (atomically), then notify after releasing locks, ideally asynchronously. At scale the Observer becomes a Kafka topic: the order service writes a transition event and subscribers consume it independently, at-least-once, with idempotent handlers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• In-process Observer: CopyOnWriteArrayList<OrderListener>; reads are lock-free; callbacks run on the caller thread unless dispatched.
  • Isolation: wrap each listener in try/catch so one failure does not stop others.
  • Outbox pattern: write the event in the same DB transaction as the status update, and a relay publishes to Kafka, so a crash cannot lose notifications.
moveTo(): CAS status -> publish event
           |-> push worker
           |-> tablet worker     (each consumes independently)
           |-> analytics

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• synchronized method that also calls listeners.
  • A listener that calls back into Order and deadlocks or re-enters.
  • Assuming events arrive exactly once and in order across consumers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What ordering guarantee do you need? -> Per order: partition Kafka by orderId.
  2. What if a listener throws? -> Isolate, log, retry with backoff, dead-letter.
  3. Why outbox? -> Atomic status change plus event; avoids dual-write inconsistency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Observer decouples". Senior: moves notifications out of locks, isolates failures, discusses at-least-once delivery, idempotent handlers and the outbox.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A slow SMS vendor made every order accept take 6 seconds because the listener ran under the order lock.

questions.contextHtml: After scaling to 8 app servers, dinner peak (3,000 orders/s city-wide) shows two orders assigned the same driver D17 within 40 ms. The code: freeDrivers.poll() on a ConcurrentLinkedQueue in each JVM, seeded from the same driver table on startup. Driver app shows two simultaneous pickups. Unit tests pass (single JVM).
questions.promptHtml: Why does it happen, how do you fix it, and how do you test it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds synchronized or a bigger lock in the JVM.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is driver state in the DB or per-JVM memory? How are free drivers decided (location, shift)? What is the rate of driver state changes? Is there a driver-location service?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin dispatch for a city to a single server (sticky routing) or add a DB-level claim before accepting an assignment.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Each JVM has its own copy of the free pool: poll() is atomic per queue but not across queues (matches the symptom). (b) A retry duplicated dispatch for the same order: check idempotency. (c) Clock skew in logs: red herring.
  4. How I'd verify: Query assignments grouped by driver with overlapping active orders; compare the order of events across servers by DB timestamps.
  5. Root cause: Process-local state is used as a shared resource.
  6. Fix: One atomic claim in the shared store: UPDATE driver SET current_order=? WHERE id=? AND current_order IS NULL, rows affected 1 means claimed; if 0, try the next candidate. Or Redis SET driver:D17:lock order EX 30 NX. Keep the assignment strategy pure (returns candidates in preference order); the claim loop is in FoodService.
  7. Prevention: Integration test with two service instances and a shared Postgres, 100 parallel dispatches, asserting no driver has two active orders; a DB constraint (unique on active driver assignment).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A per-driver DB claim adds a round trip (about 1 to 2 ms) but gives correctness; I would not use a global distributed lock on the whole pool (a bottleneck at 3,000 orders/s) and would not keep the free list in one server's RAM as the source of truth.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Claim succeeds but the driver rejects the offer? -> Release with a conditional update and try the next candidate; keep an offer expiry.
  • Hot city shard: all orders try the same top drivers? -> Randomize among the top K or use SKIP LOCKED.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite scale-out incident where logic that was correct on one server double-assigned drivers on the first night with two, and no unit test could have caught it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: in-JVM synchronized.
  • Hire: shared-store conditional claim and next-candidate loop.
  • Strong hire: DB constraint, offer expiry, SKIP LOCKED for hot contention, integration test with multiple instances.

questions.contextHtml: Rule: if the restaurant has not accepted within 3 minutes, auto-cancel and refund. A first version starts a Thread.sleep(180000) thread per order; at dinner peak (3,000 orders/s) this means about 540,000 sleeping threads and the JVM dies. Orders that were accepted still get cancelled sometimes ("cancel if still PLACED" implemented as a check then a cancel).
questions.promptHtml: Redesign the timeout mechanism and make the cancellation correct.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increases heap or uses a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor per order and calls it a day, ignoring restarts and the check-then-act bug.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the timeout precise to the second or approximate (a few seconds is fine)? Must it survive a restart? Multiple servers? Do we also warn the restaurant at 2 minutes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the thread-per-order path; run a periodic sweeper every 5 s as a stopgap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Threads are the wrong abstraction: 540,000 x 1 MB stack = 540 GB of virtual stack. (b) Cancelled-after-accepted comes from a race between accept and cancel. (c) Timer precision: red herring.
  4. How I'd verify: Thread count in the JVM, memory; a test where accept and the timer fire together.
  5. Root cause: One thread per timer, and a non-atomic check-then-cancel.
  6. Fix: Store acceptDeadline = placedAt + 3 min with the order. A single scheduler (hashed wheel timer or a DB query) periodically selects status='PLACED' AND acceptDeadline < now() LIMIT 1000 and cancels each with the conditional update UPDATE orders SET status='CANCELLED' WHERE id=? AND status='PLACED'; a zero row count means the restaurant already accepted, so nothing happens. Survives restarts because state is in the DB. Alternatively Kafka delay topics or Redis sorted set keyed by deadline.
  7. Prevention: Metrics for overdue orders and sweeper lag; a test that accepts at deadline minus 1 ms versus plus 1 ms; make the sweeper idempotent so two servers running it is safe.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The sweeper has a few seconds of lateness; that is fine for a 3-minute rule. I would not use Thread.sleep per order or in-memory timers for something that must survive a restart. At 3,000 orders per second with a 3-minute window, about 540,000 orders are pending at once (verify with real accept rates, since most are accepted in under a minute), so index (status, accept_deadline) and keep the batch size bounded.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Restaurant accepts exactly at the deadline? -> Whichever conditional update runs first wins; the other changes zero rows.
  • Retry storms on refund failure? -> The cancel and refund request are separate events; refund is retried idempotently with an idempotency key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident where an in-memory timer lost all pending cancellations on a deploy, leaving thousands of orders hanging in PLACED until support noticed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: thread per order.
  • Hire: deadline stored plus sweeper, conditional cancel.
  • Strong hire: index and batch sizing, restart safety, idempotent refund, boundary test and delay-queue alternatives.
